# Diagnosing Zero Coolant Flow in a Heated Radiator System

A burst upper radiator hose on a 1995 GMC Sierra 5.7L is a classic symptom of unmanaged thermal expansion, but the persistent lack of flow after replacing major components suggests the physics of the cooling loop have been disrupted rather than simply fixed. You have installed new hoses, a thermostat, a water pump, and flushed the system. You have also removed the thermostat to verify flow, yet the coolant remains stagnant in the radiator. This specific behaviorâstagnation even with the restriction valve openâindicates a blockage downstream or an airlock preventing circulation.

When you remove the thermostat completely, the engine block should still push fluid through the upper hose into the radiator. If the water sits there, gravity and pump pressure are being defeated by something else. The most common culprit in this scenario is a collapsed lower intake elbow or a clogged heater core acting as a restriction. In older vehicles like the Sierra 5.7L, the plastic intake manifold runners can soften and collapse under heat, creating a physical bottleneck that looks like a pump failure but is actually a plumbing obstruction.

Before condemning the water pump again, inspect the lower radiator hose connection at the engine block. If the internal ribbing of the hose has collapsed or if there is debris from the previous burst hose lodged in the tank neck, the fluid cannot exit the radiator to recirculate. Even with a brand-new pump spinning, if the return path is obstructed, you will see zero flow at the top while the engine continues to overheat.

Another critical factor is air entrapment. When you replaced the upper hose, you likely introduced air into the system. If the bleed screw (if equipped) was not used or if the coolant level was insufficient during the fill, large pockets of air can sit in the cylinder head water jackets or the thermostat housing. Air does not conduct heat well and compresses under pressure, effectively creating a seal that stops flow. The fact that removing the thermostat didn't resolve it suggests the air might be trapped past the thermostat housing, possibly in the intake manifold or near the freeze plugs.

You should also verify the condition of the freeze plugs (core bolts) on the block. If any of these have blown internally during the initial overheating event, coolant can leak into the oil passages or cylinder bores rather than circulating through the radiator. This internal leakage would result in zero visible flow through the external hoses despite the pump running. Check for milky oil or white exhaust smoke as secondary confirmation of this failure mode.

Finally, consider the integrity of the new water pump impeller. If the hub wasn't seated correctly or if the gasket was not replaced with a sealant-free option (using only RTV in the correct spot), coolant can bypass the impeller entirely. This creates a "dead head" scenario where the pump appears to turn but moves no fluid. To test this, run the engine with the radiator cap off and feel the upper hose temperature while the lower hose is cold; if both are hot or neither is moving, the loop is broken.

If the block is clear, the pump is sealed, and there is no air lock, the issue may be a collapsed internal passage in the newly installed thermostat housing itself. Sometimes aftermarket housings have thinner walls that deform under heat, restricting flow even without the spring-loaded valve engaged. Ensure you are using a reputable brand for the thermostat assembly rather than a generic unit that might not meet OEM tolerances.
